title: Zero integral of a compactly supported divergence

content.display_title: Zero integral of a compactly supported divergence
content.one_sentence_role: Makes all faces in a box divergence formula vanish by placing the support strictly inside the box.
content.natural_language_statement:
Fix $n\geq1$. Let $F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ and have compact topological support. Let $DF(x)$ denote the real Fréchet derivative and $e_j$ the $j$th standard coordinate vector. Write
$$F_j(x):=(F(x))_j,\qquad
\partial_jF_j(x):=(DF(x)e_j)_j,\qquad
\operatorname{div}F(x):=\sum_{j=1}^n\partial_jF_j(x).$$
For Lebesgue measure on the coordinate space,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\operatorname{div}F(x)\,dx=0.$$
content.assumptions:
The support convention throughout this card is
$$\operatorname{supp}F:=\overline{\{x\in\mathbb R^n:F(x)\ne0\}}.$$
This closed set is assumed compact. The differentiability hypothesis is exactly $C^1$. The domain has its coordinate sup norm. No externally specified integration domain or boundary-regularity assumption is needed.
content.conclusion: The divergence is integrable and its whole-space integral vanishes. Compact support is imposed on $F$, which also forces the divergence to vanish off that support.
content.proof_summary: Choose a box with the support strictly inside it. Write the box divergence formula as a sum of upper-face minus lower-face integrals. Each face value is zero, and the divergence is zero outside the box, so the whole-space integral is zero.

proof_steps.text:
**Enclose the support and justify integrability.** Choose $R>0$ such that
$$\operatorname{supp}F\subset(-R,R)^n,\qquad Q=[-R,R]^n.$$
If $x\notin\operatorname{supp}F$, some neighborhood of $x$ is disjoint from the nonzero set of $F$. On that neighborhood $F=0$, and hence $DF(x)=0$. Therefore
$$x\notin\operatorname{supp}F\ \Longrightarrow\ \partial_jF_j(x)=0\ \text{for every }j
\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{div}F(x)=0.$$
The divergence is continuous because $F$ is $C^1$, so it is integrable on compact $Q$. It is zero on $Q^c$, and is therefore integrable on $\mathbb R^n$ as well.

**Spell out the face formula.** Fix $i$. Let $Q_{\widehat i}=\prod_{k\ne i}[-R,R]$ and write $y=(y_k)_{k\ne i}$. Insert the missing coordinate by
$$\bigl(\iota_i(t,y)\bigr)_k=
\begin{cases}t,&k=i,\\y_k,&k\ne i.\end{cases}$$
For fixed $y$, the scalar function $t\mapsto F_i(\iota_i(t,y))$ is $C^1$ and
$$\frac{d}{dt}F_i(\iota_i(t,y))
=(DF(\iota_i(t,y))e_i)_i=\partial_iF_i(\iota_i(t,y)).$$
The face expression in the box divergence theorem is precisely the following repeated-integral calculation (Fubini on the compact box, followed by the one-dimensional fundamental theorem of calculus):
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_Q\partial_iF_i(x)\,dx
&=\int_{Q_{\widehat i}}\left[\int_{-R}^{R}
\frac{d}{dt}F_i(\iota_i(t,y))\,dt\right]dy\\
&=\int_{Q_{\widehat i}}\left[F_i(\iota_i(R,y))-F_i(\iota_i(-R,y))\right]dy.
\end{aligned}$$
Sum over $i$ to obtain $\int_Q\operatorname{div}F$. In the source this sum is obtained directly from the cited box divergence theorem: $C^1$ supplies continuity and a derivative everywhere, the exceptional set is empty, and Step 1 supplies integrability. The calculation above explains its face terms.

**Set the face values to zero and pass to the whole space.** The $i$th coordinate of $\iota_i(\pm R,y)$ is $\pm R$. Hence
$$\iota_i(\pm R,y)\notin(-R,R)^n
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\iota_i(\pm R,y)\notin\operatorname{supp}F
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F_i(\iota_i(\pm R,y))=0.$$
Each integrand in the last line of Step 2 is thus $0-0$. Since Step 1 also gives $\operatorname{div}F=0$ on $Q^c$,
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_{\mathbb R^n}\operatorname{div}F
&=\int_Q\operatorname{div}F+\int_{Q^c}\operatorname{div}F\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n\int_{Q_{\widehat i}}(0-0)\,dy+0=0.
\end{aligned}$$
For $n=1$, $Q_{\widehat i}$ is the zero-dimensional one-point product; the formula is simply the difference of the two endpoint values.

content.lean_realization_notes: For $n=1$ the two faces are endpoints and the same formula is the fundamental theorem of calculus. The source represents face coordinates by inserting one fixed coordinate into an $(n-1)$-tuple.
